newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani missing woman mystery unresolved.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani missing woman mystery unresolved.

text.p: The mystery of a Pakistani woman who went missing a few days after winning an 11-month court battle against her father's challenge to her love marriage remains unresolved, police said on Saturday.
Saima Waheed's disappearance has given a sensational twist to a case which had symbolised the struggle between Moslem conservatives and women's rights advocates in Pakistan.
"No one has approached us or registered a kidnapping case in connection with Saima Waheed," a senior police officer told Reuters by telephone from Lahore.
Saima was last seen on Thursday when she left a women's shelter where she had spent 11 months under a court order, but failed to join her husband Arshad Ahmad, a college lecturer.
Her lawyer Asma Jahangir, who is also chairperson of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, said she could not explain what had happened, but believed Saima had been kidnapped.
"I feel certain that no one can get away with this high-handedness and the mystery will solve itself and those responsible will come to the limelight," Jahangir said.
On Friday, Saima's husband accused his own lawyer Abid Saqi of taking away his wife after her release from the shelter, but Saqi denied this, saying he had handed her over to his client.

On Monday the Lahore High Court upheld Saima's marriage in a 2-1 verdict, ruling it valid in the eyes of Islam even though it occurred against the will of her father, Abdul Waheed Ropri, a member of the militant Sunni Moslem Ahle Hadith organisation.

Ropri accused Jahangir on Friday of playing a "dirty role" and brain-washing his daughter at the behest of foreign governments he said had paid Jahangir to play up the case in the interests of undermining Islam and family values.

Jahangir said she had fulfilled her obligations as a lawyer, but the conclusion of the case had ended her role. "I can't say what happened later which forced Saima to change her mind. Was it fear or something else, I don't know," she said.
However, Jahangir said it was strange that none of those involved had filed a police report about Saima's disappearance.
She dismissed Ropri's allegations that she had received money from foreign governments as "malicious and absurd".
